1:
Why Ahab reported Carmel to Jezebel divides them flatly. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) holds he told her not to convince but to exasperate, his conscience retaining too much of the Israelite to let him persecute Elijah himself: he reported not what God had done but what Elijah had done, as though the man had fetched fire from heaven by a spell, and he calls the slain priests simply the prophets, as if none but they deserved the name, never noticing it was reprisal for Jezebel’s killing of God’s own. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) answers in six words, that Ahab told her probably with no evil design against Elijah. That she warned rather than struck is read as weakness: Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) call it the impotence of a woman’s rage, since she wanted only to be rid of him, unable to kill him partly for the people, enthusiastic in his favour, and partly for the king, on whom Carmel had not been without salutary effect.

The flight draws four verdicts. Henry will not excuse it: shall we praise him for this? We praise him not. He who stood undaunted amid the terrors of heaven and earth trembles at the menaces of a proud passionate woman — Lord, what is man. John Gill (reformed) turns the contrast into doctrine, that one who faced four hundred and fifty priests should fear a single woman shows the courage he had was of the Lord and not of himself. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads temperament: the sudden reaction of despondency, strange as it looks to superficial observation, is characteristic of an impulsive and vehement nature whose blow had been struck as it thought triumphantly, and which now feels a cool unrelenting antagonism only embittered by all that passed. Clarke blames frustrated expectation, Elijah having thought Carmel would convert the whole court and country.

Beersheba is read for what it discloses. Keil and Delitzsch take the note that it belonged to Judah as showing he meant to quit Israel altogether, the scene of his labours, as Jeremiah in a like conflict wished to leave his people; Ellicott finds the note significant the other way, Judah being then in half-dependent alliance with Israel, so that even under Jehoshaphat Elijah might not be safe there though his servant could stay. On the words under the tree Ellicott is at his best: the exclamation is characteristic, for evidently Elijah had hoped he was better than his fathers, singled out beyond all before him to be the victorious champion of a great crisis, he and he alone; now he thinks that hope vain and asks why he should live when the rest of the prophets have died.

The provision draws out the homely and the large. Gill, following Bochart, has the cake baked on hot stones after the eastern manner, a thing Keil and Delitzsch report still a favourite with the Bedouins; and from the journey they draw the inference that governs it, that since the angel never said where to go, yet he walked to Horeb, he must have intended from the first to go into the desert and see whether the Lord would acknowledge him further, reading in the strength given him an indication to seek the mountain where God once spoke to Moses. Clarke notes that the fast matched Moses’s there and our Lord’s in the wilderness. Ellicott doubts the forty days were walking at all, the distance being some two hundred miles, and takes them for an interval of retirement in which the prophet’s spirit might be calmed; he observes too how rarely angels appear in the prophetic period, as though their ministry had passed to the prophetic mission itself, so that here the angel is auxiliary to the prophet, as the angel of the Agony to the Prophet of prophets.
9:
What doest thou here, Elijah, is heard three ways. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) deny any rebuke in it: the question did not involve a reproof, as though Elijah had nothing to do there, but was simply intended to draw out the thoughts and feelings of his heart. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) hears it reproving twice over, for the fleeing and for the fixing. He lays the emphasis on the pronoun, this cowardice being more excusable in another: should such a man as I flee? Howl, fir-trees, if the cedars be thus shaken. Then: is this a place for a prophet of the Lord to lodge in, is this a time for such men to retreat, when the public has such need of them? In his earlier retirement he blessed a widow at Sarepta; here he had no opportunity of doing good. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) leaves it open, asking only whether it is a reproach for fleeing from Jezebel through what some call unbelieving fears.

Which cave is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch take the definite article to point back to the cleft of the rock where Moses stood while the glory of Jehovah passed by. John Gill (reformed) reports the Jewish writers of the same mind, then refuses it on the text’s own showing: if this were that cleft there would have been no need for Elijah to go forth and stand upon the mount when the Lord passed by. Gill has it shown to travellers still at the foot of Sinai, enclosed in a granite church. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) offers the alternative that the article is anticipatory, naming not a cave already famous but the one Elijah’s sojourn was to make so. Henry notices the reversal: Moses was put into the cave when the glory passed, Elijah called out of it.

The complaint is weighed quite differently. Henry defends it, asking that the retreat be imputed not to want of zeal but to despair of success, since while there was hope he had been jealous for the Lord, and now had laboured in vain; though Henry grants that the apostle calls this making intercession against Israel, the advocate necessitated at last to be his people’s accuser. Keil and Delitzsch find in it not only the greatest despair but a carnal zeal that would gladly have called down immediate vengeance upon all idolaters, and a tacit reproof that God had looked on so long. Ellicott calls it impatient self-exculpation and even remonstrance: he had been jealous for the Lord, yet the Lord had not been jealous for himself. Ellicott sets it beside Isaiah’s cry, Jonah’s anger, and the message from prison, finding in the Elias of the New Testament the same despondent impatience.

On the theophany Ellicott is the fullest. He reads it against the two earlier manifestations here: to the people, power made visible, the whirlwind and fire being the natural clothing of the terrors of the Law and the only signs their hearts were then prepared for; to Moses, not the divine majesty but the Name, merciful and gracious. Elijah’s vision contrasts with the first and harmonises with the second, disclaiming the display of vengeance he had by implication craved. Clarke offers the same law-and-gospel reading, the terrors only introducing the still small voice, but reports the naturalistic alternative, that the sequence describes a real earthquake in order, concluding that the exciting cause was supernatural even so. Gill and Clarke both pass on the Targum’s hosts of angels of wind, commotion and fire, and its rendering of the voice as a singing in silence, a sound with which no other was mingled. Henry draws the lesson from what moved him: the wind and earthquake and fire did not make him cover his face, but the still voice did, gracious souls being more affected by mercies than by terrors.
15:
The commission is read as an answer to both halves of the complaint. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds in it an indirect double rebuke: the cry that he was not better than his fathers, which implied that he stood out beyond all others to meet the stern requirements of the time, is met by the charge to delegate the work of vengeance to others; and the complaint that he alone was left is met by the revelation of a faithful remnant unknown to him, perhaps unknown to one another, but known and loved by God. John Gill (reformed) has him bidden back the way he came, but passes on the suggestion of Fortunatus Schacchus that the phrase means no more than a return to preaching the law and reclaiming men from the error of their ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) notes that the road given him is not one on which he would be likely to meet Jezebel.

That Elijah performed only part of what he was told is turned to account. Gill observes that Jehu was anointed by Elisha, not Elijah, and that being done at his order it was as if he had done it himself, unless the man was anointed twice. Ellicott makes the gap evidence: Elijah fulfilled in person only the call of Elisha, and this apparently imperfect correspondence of the event to the charge is a strong indication of the historical character of the narrative. He adds that no anointing of Elisha is recorded, and that nowhere else is a prophet’s anointing mentioned: the rite began with the priests and passed to the kings, and whether prophets took the oil at all, or whether, as in the Prophet of prophets, the anointing with the Holy Ghost superseded the outward sign, he says we do not know.

The sword given to Elisha is the difficulty. Clarke denies that Elisha ever used a sword or commissioned one, and settles the matter by chronology: Elisha was prophet before Hazael was king, and Hazael king before Jehu, so the order of time here is not to be regarded, and the sense is that the three shall be ministers of vengeance. Ellicott grants that the mission was plainly not one of vengeance, Elisha having to destroy enmity but not to slay the enemies of God, and again makes the trouble a mark of accuracy: the mission is probably described in the terms in which Elijah would best understand it, for his spirit was for war, and he could hardly have conceived how his work was to be completed by weapons of peace in his successor’s hand.

The remnant and the kiss are read for their realism. Clarke takes the seven thousand for many thousands, seven being a number of perfection, and suspects that while the court and the multitudes had gone after Baal the majority of the common people still worshipped the God of their fathers in secret. Ellicott would render it I leave, or will leave, through all this vengeance, and sets the seven thousand beside the remnant sealed in the visions of Ezekiel and of the Revelation. On the kissing, Ellicott describes the worshipper bowing the knee on first approach and on nearer access kissing the image, or the altar, or the threshold. Clarke traces adoration itself to the gesture, the word being compounded of the Latin for to and for mouth, and gathers his witnesses: Pliny, that in adoration we kiss the right hand and turn the whole body about; Cicero, on a statue of Hercules whose chin and lips were worn smooth by the kisses of worshippers; and his own observation of old paintings of the saints whose lips had been literally worn away by devotees.
19:
Where Elisha was found carries weight. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) presses it hardest: he was found not in the schools of the prophets but in the field, not reading nor praying nor sacrificing but ploughing, and though master of the ground and oxen and servants he thought it no disparagement to lay his own hand to the plough — idleness is no man’s honour, nor is husbandry any man’s disgrace. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reckons the cost instead, so large an estate meaning that he obeyed at considerable secular loss. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) hears in the quiet simplicity of this call a contrast with the sudden and mysterious appearance of Elijah himself, while John Gill (reformed) measures the journey, Bunting computing Abelmeholah at a hundred and fifty-six miles.

The mantle is read as vocation, as adoption, and as ancestor of a later rite. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put it simply, that the prophet’s cloak was the sign of the prophet’s vocation, so that throwing it was a symbol of the call. Clarke allows it may mark the prophetic office or only service to the prophet,. Ellicott reports that the act is said to have been part of the form of adopting a child, which would give its significance here. Henry takes it for friendship, Elijah receiving him under his mantle as under his care, or for his being clothed with his master’s spirit as Moses put his honour upon Joshua; at the ascent the mantle came to him entire. Clarke ventures furthest, conjecturing that the popes borrowed from this act the ceremony of the pall, and retailing from Durandus the pall as signifying the plenitude of ecclesiastical power.

What have I done to thee is where they part. Keil and Delitzsch read bare permission, the words meaning only that Elijah had not wanted to put any constraint upon him. Clarke makes it a disclaimer of agency: the call is not from me but from God, and to him art thou accountable. Ellicott hears half-ironical rebuke of what seemed hesitation, go back if thou wilt, what have I done to constrain thee, comparing the request made to our Lord in the gospel, and finding in both a stern rejection of half-hearted service. Henry denies that comparison outright: this was no excuse for delay, like the request of the man who would first bid farewell to those at home, but only a reservation of the duty owed to a father and mother. For Henry the reply preserves the will: Elijah refuses to force him, letting him count the cost and make it his own act, since the efficacy of grace leaves the native liberty of man’s will intact, so that the good are good of choice, not pressed men but volunteers.

The feast and the service after it are read for what they cost. Keil and Delitzsch describe it plainly: the pair he had ploughed with slaughtered, the flesh boiled with the plough, a farewell meal for his own people, then the following of Elijah as his assistant. Clarke takes the burning of the implements for a token that he had abandoned secular life, and that such a call never supersedes the duties of filial affection, the parents making no attempt to hinder him. Ellicott sets the meal beside Matthew’s, a feast of farewell to his home and of homage to his new master, and notes what he accepted: from a master he became a servant, content to be known even in his own prophetic days as he that poured water on the hands of Elijah. Henry reads the feast as evidence that the call was welcome, though it exposed him to Jezebel’s party, and draws the lesson that those who would be fit to teach must have time to learn, and those who hope to rule must first stoop and serve.
